title: Clarifying Questions Before You Code
summary: The questions worth asking in the first two minutes are the ones whose answer changes your approach. Learn which constraint and ambiguity questions earn their keep, and which ones just stall.

slides.markdown:
Interviewers watch the first two minutes closer than any other part of the interview, because it's the only part where you're not yet committed to an approach. **The questions you ask before writing code are themselves a signal** — they show whether you read constraints for what they imply, or just skim them.

Good clarifying questions share one property: **the answer changes what you build.** "Can the array be empty?" changes your code. "What language should I use?" changes nothing about the algorithm.

This topic is about picking the first kind and skipping the second — fast, in under two minutes, without turning it into an interrogation.

slides.sectionTitle: Constraint questions that change the algorithm
slides.markdown:
Four constraints decide which algorithm is even legal, so ask about them before you commit to one:

- **Input size (n).** Determines the complexity you're allowed to ship — see the next slide.
- **Value range.** "Can values be negative?" kills a bit-trick or an XOR-based solution that assumes unsigned integers. "Are values bounded, like 0–255?" opens up counting sort or a fixed-size array instead of a hash map.
- **Sortedness.** A sorted input turns an O(n) scan into an O(log n) binary search, or makes two pointers viable instead of a hash set.
- **Duplicates.** "Are there duplicate keys?" changes whether you need a `Set` or a `Counter`, and whether "the kth largest" is even well-defined.

Each of these is a fork in your approach, not a detail — ask before you pick a data structure, not after.

slides.sectionTitle: Ambiguity questions that change the answer
slides.markdown:
Some inputs don't change the algorithm's shape, but do change what the *correct output* is. Get these wrong and your working code returns a wrong answer on the interviewer's hidden test:

- **Empty input.** Does an empty array return `0`, `-1`, `null`, or throw? All four are defensible; only one is what they want.
- **A single element.** Is `[5]` a valid "pair"? Is a one-node tree "balanced"? Edge-of-one cases catch a surprising fraction of off-by-ones.
- **Negative numbers.** "Largest subarray sum" reads differently if every number can be negative — the answer might legitimately be negative too.
- **Ties.** "Find the first longest substring" versus "find any longest substring" are different specs when two candidates tie for longest.

Asking these up front turns a guess into a specification, and the interviewer will tell you which one they actually meant.

slides.subTitle: The five-second habit
slides.markdown:
Before proposing an approach, **restate the problem in your own words** and pause for a nod. This is one sentence, not a summary of your plan:

> "So I need to find, for every position, the nearest element to its left that's smaller — and return -1 where there isn't one. Is that right?"

This does three things at once: it surfaces a misunderstanding while it's still cheap to fix, it gives the interviewer a natural moment to correct a constraint you misread, and it buys you a few seconds to actually think about the approach while sounding productive rather than silent.

Skip this and the failure mode is expensive: you solve the problem you *assumed* was asked, discover the mismatch after ten minutes of coding, and now you're rebuilding under a worse time crunch than if you'd asked at second zero.

slides.sectionTitle: Reading constraint sizes as a complexity budget
slides.subTitle: n tells you the answer before you design it
slides.markdown:
The stated bound on **n** is the single highest-signal number in the prompt — read it as a direct instruction about which complexity is expected, before you design anything:

| Constraint | What it's telling you |
|---|---|
| n ≤ 10 – 20 | Exponential is fine — bitmask DP, subsets, backtracking |
| n ≤ 500 – 1,000 | O(n²) or O(n² log n) is intended |
| n ≤ 10^5 – 10^6 | You need O(n log n) or better — a nested loop will time out |
| n ≤ 10^9 or unbounded | O(log n) or O(1) only — think binary search on the answer, math, or two pointers |

If you don't see a bound stated, ask for one — "roughly how large can n get?" — because the answer tells you whether to even consider your first instinct. A candidate who writes an O(n²) solution against `n ≤ 10^6` without ever reading the constraint looks like they didn't think about scale at all, even if the logic is correct.

slides.sectionTitle: A question that earns its keep vs. one that doesn't
slides.subTitle: "Is it sorted?" vs. "Which language?"
slides.markdown:
Compare two real opening questions:

- **"Can I assume the array is sorted?"** — the answer directly decides between an O(n) hash-set approach and an O(log n) two-pointer or binary-search approach. Whatever they say, your next sentence changes.
- **"What language should I use?"** — usually already decided by the platform, and even when it's open, your algorithm doesn't move an inch either way. It's stalling dressed as diligence.

The test that separates them: **if you can already picture both branches of your plan changing based on the answer, ask it. If you'd give the same solution either way, it isn't a clarifying question — it's noise**, and interviewers notice when the first two minutes are spent on questions that don't affect anything.

slides.sectionTitle: Asking a question that changes nothing
slides.markdown:
A subtler version of the same mistake: asking a *real-sounding* constraint question whose answer doesn't actually move your approach.

"Should I optimize for time or space?" sounds sharp, but if you don't yet have two candidate solutions with a genuine time/space trade-off between them, the question has nothing to attach to — you're asking the interviewer to do your design thinking for you.

Before asking any question, silently check: **"what do I do differently for each possible answer?"** If you can't name two different plans, don't ask it yet — get further into the problem first, then ask once the fork actually exists.

The opposite failure is worse than asking too many questions: **silently assuming** a convenient property — sortedness, no duplicates, non-negative values — and coding as if the interviewer confirmed it.

This fails in two ways. If the assumption is wrong, your solution is wrong on a case the interviewer definitely tests. If the assumption happens to be *right*, the interviewer still doesn't know you knew you were assuming it — from their side, you got lucky, not that you reasoned about it.

The fix costs one sentence: **"I'll assume the array can contain duplicates unless you say otherwise"** turns a silent guess into a stated, defensible choice — and gives them a two-second window to correct you before you've written a line of code.

slides.sectionTitle: How many questions, and when to stop
slides.subTitle: Pacing the first two minutes
slides.markdown:
Two or three sharp questions read as diligence. Six or seven read as stalling, even if every one of them is individually reasonable.

A workable pace: ask about **input size and value range** first — they gate the algorithm choice entirely — then ask about the one or two edge cases that are genuinely ambiguous for *this specific problem*, not a rehearsed checklist recited every time. Once you've restated the problem and covered the forks that actually matter, stop asking and start proposing an approach out loud.

The senior-level version of this skill is knowing you can keep asking **later**, mid-solution, the moment a new fork appears — "actually, one more thing: can this list be circular?" — rather than trying to front-load every possible question before writing a single line.

slides.subTitle: What this sounds like out loud
slides.markdown:
```
Candidate: Before I start — can the array be empty, and can values repeat?
Interviewer: Assume non-empty, and yes, duplicates are possible.
Candidate: Got it. And roughly how large can n get?
Interviewer: Up to about 10^5.
Candidate: Okay, so I need something better than O(n^2) — I'm thinking
           a hash set gets this to O(n) in one pass. Let me restate the
           problem first: for every element, I want the count of other
           elements smaller than it. Is that right?
Interviewer: That's right, go ahead.
```

Notice the order: constraint questions first, since they gate the whole approach, then the restate-and-confirm, and only then does coding start — all inside about thirty seconds. Nothing here is padding; every line changes or confirms something about the plan.

slides.subTitle: Beyond a memorized checklist
slides.markdown:
A fixed checklist recited from memory reads as rehearsed, and it misses problem-specific ambiguity a checklist can't anticipate. The stronger habit is reading the *specific* prompt for what it leaves open, informed by patterns you've built from practice: a string problem makes you check case-sensitivity and whitespace; a tree problem makes you check whether it's guaranteed balanced; a graph problem makes you check whether it's directed and whether it can have cycles.

After every mock or real interview, it's worth noting which clarifying question you *should* have asked but didn't — that gap is exactly what your next practice session should target. Over time this turns into instinct: you read `n ≤ 10^9`, and a complexity budget forms before you've consciously decided to think about one.
